steps.body: Liquid volume follows the pattern too: a liter holds 1,000 milliliters, so 4 L is 4,000 mL and 6,000 mL is 6 L.
steps.narration: Liquid volume follows the pattern too: a liter holds 1,000 milliliters, so 4 L is 4,000 mL and 6,000 mL is 6 L.

widget.prompt: How many milliliters in 4 liters? Hop one liter at a time.

commonLandings.feedback: Three hops reach 3,000 mL; the jug holds four liters.
Five hops overshoot — four liters is 4,000 milliliters.

widget.missFeedback: Each liter is 1,000 milliliters, so four reach 4,000.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — each liter is 1,000 milliliters, so four reach 4,000.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — four liters stops exactly at 4,000 milliliters.

cml.actionGoal: Convert between liters and milliliters and interpret remainders when containers are required.
invariants: One liter is exactly 1,000 milliliters; a leftover amount needs another container when all liquid must be carried.
misconceptions: Dropping a remainder when the context requires every liter to be carried.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the unit got ten times smaller, what would happen to the number that measures the same object?

widget.prompt: A jug measures 6 liters, and each liter is 1000 milliliters. Compute 6 × 1000.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding mixes a quantity with a rate. Each of the 6 liters contributes 1000 milliliters, so they multiply.
That divided. Going to the SMALLER unit needs more of them, so the number must grow.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the quantity and the conversion factor, then decide whether the count should grow or shrink.

widget.prompt: Apply the liquid-volume relationship to a new value: how many milliliters are in 3 liters?

commonLandings.feedback: Two hops represent two liters; three liters needs one more hop.
Four hops overshoot; three liters is 3,000 milliliters.

widget.missFeedback: Three equal hops of 1,000 milliliters land at 3,000 milliliters.
widget.successFeedback: 3,000 milliliters — three liter-hops of 1,000 milliliters each.
widget.lowFeedback: This landing is short of three complete liter-hops.
widget.highFeedback: This landing is past three complete liter-hops.

widget.prompt: Apply without the opening model: A jug measures 7000 milliliters, and each liter is 1000 milliliters. Compute 7000 ÷ 1000.

commonErrors.feedback: 7000 is the count in milliliters. Switching to the bigger liter must make the NUMBER smaller.
That multiplied. Going to the BIGGER unit needs fewer of them, so divide.

widget.prompt: Retrieve or diagnose in a new form: 56 liters are poured into 6-liter jugs. Every liter must be carried. How many jugs are needed?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 full jugs leave 2 liters behind, and every liter has to travel.
2 is the leftover liquid, not a count of jugs.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide by the container size; if any amount remains, one more container is required.

concept.body: For multiplicatively related units, identify the factor and direction. Here, 1 liter equals 1,000 milliliters.
concept.narration: For multiplicatively related units, identify the factor and direction. Here, 1 liter equals 1,000 milliliters.

widget.prompt: A bottle holds 8 liters, and 1 liter equals 1000 milliliters. Multiply to find how many milliliters that is.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding mixes a quantity with a rate. Each of the 8 liters needs its own factor of 1000, not one addition.
That kept the liter count. Milliliters are the smaller unit, so the number must grow by the factor of 1000.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the constant factor linking the units: multiply the liter count by 1,000.
